item.title: Systematic Review of Geographical Information Systems and Remote Sensing in Assessing Climate‐Induced Water Resource Scarcity
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Climate change intensifies extreme precipitation, raises temperatures, and disrupts hydrological regimes, placing growing pressure on water resources. Remote sensing (RS) and geographic information systems (GIS) are widely used to monitor hydrological processes; however, many studies address isolated components of the water cycle, limiting a comprehensive understanding of climate‐driven water scarcity. This systematic review evaluates the application of RS and GIS in assessing climate‐related water resource decline. Using the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, it is found that there are 2034 publications from 2016 to 2025 in Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, and 319 peer‐reviewed articles were suitable for detailed analysis. Bibliometric and keyword time‐overlay analyzes using VOSviewer reveal evolving research themes and methodological convergence. Findings show strong links between thematic focus and water resource type, a shift toward data‐driven methods, including machine learning and cloud platforms such as Google Earth Engine, and persistent challenges in cross‐scale transferability and linking observed depletion to climatic indicators. This review is the first to apply PRISMA 2020 to the GIS/RS + climate + water scarcity axis, integrate bibliometric clustering analysis with chi‐square testing, and map methodological differences across scales. It also addresses a gap in the literature by presenting a comprehensive synthesis that examines climate change, water scarcity, and GIS/RS methodology together within a single systematic framework across different water resource types and spatial scales.

ABSTRACT

Climate change intensifies extreme precipitation, raises temperatures, and disrupts hydrological regimes, placing growing pressure on water resources. Remote sensing (RS) and geographic information systems (GIS) are widely used to monitor hydrological processes; however, many studies address isolated components of the water cycle, limiting a comprehensive understanding of climate-driven water scarcity. This systematic review evaluates the application of RS and GIS in assessing climate-related water resource decline. Using the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, it is found that there are 2034 publications from 2016 to 2025 in Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, and 319 peer-reviewed articles were suitable for detailed analysis. Bibliometric and keyword time-overlay analyzes using VOSviewer reveal evolving research themes and methodological convergence. Findings show strong links between thematic focus and water resource type, a shift toward data-driven methods, including machine learning and cloud platforms such as Google Earth Engine, and persistent challenges in cross-scale transferability and linking observed depletion to climatic indicators. This review is the first to apply PRISMA 2020 to the GIS/RS + climate + water scarcity axis, integrate bibliometric clustering analysis with chi-square testing, and map methodological differences across scales. It also addresses a gap in the literature by presenting a comprehensive synthesis that examines climate change, water scarcity, and GIS/RS methodology together within a single systematic framework across different water resource types and spatial scales.

item.title: Automated Construction of Geospatial Analysis Workflows: Recursive Solving of Elementary Modeling Questions Adaptive to Workflow Construction Contexts
item.description: Transactions in GIS, Volume 30, Issue 7, November 2026.
item.dc:description: ABSTRACT Geospatial analysis workflows are widely used to address complex geographic problems, but their construction is challenging due to dynamic contextual factors like the characteristics of the study area, geo‐models, and datasets during construction process. Current automated approaches typically focus on the workflow executability, neglecting such dynamic influences—defined in this paper as “workflow construction contexts.” This ignorance undermines the rationality and accuracy of workflow modeling. To address this limitation, we propose a new automated approach adaptive to workflow construction contexts, which recursively decomposes the workflow construction process into elementary modeling questions (EQs). This allows the dynamic contexts to be characterized based on pre‐formalized modeling knowledge, enabling the automated construction of appropriate workflows. Implemented in a prototype system with a knowledge graph, our approach is validated through a digital soil mapping case study. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach can successfully construct distinct, context‐specific workflow structures that adaptively match different contexts, thus significantly enhancing the rationality and feasibility of geospatial analysis workflows.
item.content:encoded:
ABSTRACT

Geospatial analysis workflows are widely used to address complex geographic problems, but their construction is challenging due to dynamic contextual factors like the characteristics of the study area, geo-models, and datasets during construction process. Current automated approaches typically focus on the workflow executability, neglecting such dynamic influences—defined in this paper as “workflow construction contexts.” This ignorance undermines the rationality and accuracy of workflow modeling. To address this limitation, we propose a new automated approach adaptive to workflow construction contexts, which recursively decomposes the workflow construction process into elementary modeling questions (EQs). This allows the dynamic contexts to be characterized based on pre-formalized modeling knowledge, enabling the automated construction of appropriate workflows. Implemented in a prototype system with a knowledge graph, our approach is validated through a digital soil mapping case study. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach can successfully construct distinct, context-specific workflow structures that adaptively match different contexts, thus significantly enhancing the rationality and feasibility of geospatial analysis workflows.
